job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Bilal Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can give me the public version and the private one. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in artificial intelligence at Redfield University, and I live in a student block ten minutes from the lab. I start around nine, usually by asking an AI assistant to explain whatever paper I'm reading, then I code in the afternoon. Evenings I run a small Discord server where about 200 students swap project ideas, and I do some tutoring for pocket money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your degree, and how did it go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science, passed with an average mark. I spent too much second year building side projects instead of revising, and I had no internship because I never got past the first interview rounds. My side projects are decent though, and they're why I got into the master's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, I'll keep using it for what it's good at. I'd also say the hype was always louder than the product, but it's still a useful tool for me. Online I'd probably write a thread about what actually worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it would sting a bit, since I'm betting my master's on AI being big. But the skills are still useful if it's just a plateau. The real pressure is the same as always: I owe about 10,000 and have two months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on my side projects and finish the thesis, which is a tool that sorts student questions for a college. I'd apply to small start-ups, since they like people who ship things. I'd also charge for my tutoring, since I've been doing it for peanuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. A little deflated, but nothing scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're betting your master's on AI being big. What happens to that bet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It becomes a bet on being good at machine learning even if the buzz fades. Plenty of firms still need people who can clean data and build models. If the hype dies, I still have a skill that works, but I'd need to be honest that it's less of a golden ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you charge for tutoring now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve an hour, but I should charge twenty. My Discord friends tell me I'm underselling myself, and they're right. I'm better at building things than pricing them.

say: AI is **useful** for the right jobs, but the hype was louder than the product.
I'd write an **honest thread** about what really worked for me.
think: My master's bet is **smaller** than I hoped, but the skills still count.
I owe about **10,000** with two months of savings.
do: **Finish** the thesis tool that sorts student questions for a college.
Apply to small **start-ups** that value people who ship things.
Raise tutoring from **12** to 20 an hour.
S0.quote: If the hype dies, I still have a skill that works, but I'd need to be honest that it's less of a golden ticket.
fieldNote: Enthusiastic about AI, so a plateau is a letdown more than a threat.
Underprices himself, which shows a **confidence gap** compared with his skills.
Money pressure is **modest** but real: debt and two months of savings.

steps.text: Finish the student question sorting tool for the thesis
Apply to ten small start-ups with a link to the tool
Raise tutoring from 12 to 20 an hour

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I've been waiting for, and I'd be excited. But I'd also say loudly that we need public support, like retraining pay, because not everyone has my luck. My flatmate Ines is in accounting and she's frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm on the right side of this, but the junior jobs I'm applying to are shrinking too. Tools write what interns used to write. I need to be good enough that a firm picks me over a tool and a senior engineer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build three real projects people can use, like a tool that helps small shops answer customer emails. I'd launch it and see if anyone pays. I'd also apply for jobs the whole time and stay flexible about where. Maybe I'd go abroad if that's where the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit queasy. The same speed that helps me can drop me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the tool for small shops charge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifteen a month, I think. Shops don't have time to learn, so it has to work in an afternoon. If I get 40 customers that's enough to pay for my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Ines. What do you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I show her how to use the tools for her spreadsheets, because it's better to be in front of this than behind it. I tell my flatmate Ines that she should learn the thing before it learns her job. She doesn't like me saying that, but she's started.

say: I'm **excited**, but retraining pay is needed for people who can't move fast.
I'd say **junior jobs** are shrinking even for tool users.
think: I'm on the **right side**, but the junior jobs I want are shrinking too.
I must be **better** than a tool plus a senior engineer.
do: **Build** three real projects, including an email helper for small shops.
Launch it at **15 a month** and aim for 40 customers.
feel: **Excited** and a little queasy about the speed.
S1.quote: I tell my flatmate Ines that she should learn the thing before it learns her job.
fieldNote: Adaptive and curious, he treats disruption as a **chance** but admits the risk.
Tries to teach his accountant flatmate, a sign of **community** habits.
Anxious because the entry rungs shrink even for skilled users.

steps.text: Build three working projects and publish them online
Launch a 15 a month email helper for small shops
Use AI to automate his tutoring bookings and invoices
Apply for jobs abroad if home offers dry up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency measures, because two years is nothing. I'd call for a universal basic income trial and a rule that the gains be shared. I'd be posting about it all day, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thrilled and terrified. I'd have just finished my master's when the thinking work becomes cheap. There wouldn't be a job where I'm the human in the loop for long, but I'd be nearer the front of it than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small company straight away, offering AI set-up to local shops and schools. I'd keep tutoring, and I'd spend savings on a cheap laptop rather than rent. My parents have said I can sleep at home if it goes badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rush. I couldn't sleep and I'd also be unable to stop building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the plan work if thinking work is cheap for everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for long. People will do the set-up themselves. But there'd be a year or two where small places need a person to tell them what to do. I'd use that window to build something more lasting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said terrified. What are you afraid of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Missing my moment, and watching my parents' savings get hit too. My dad's a bus mechanic and my mum does the school canteen, and they've both put aside a little for me. I'm afraid of becoming the reason my family's small savings disappear.

say: We need **emergency measures**, such as a basic income trial.
The **gains** from AI must be shared widely.
think: I'd be thrilled and **terrified** at once, closer to the front than most.
The **human in the loop** role won't last long.
do: **Start** a small company offering AI set-up to local shops and schools.
Keep **tutoring** and buy a cheap laptop before paying rent.
Rely on my parents' **spare room** if it goes badly.
feel: A **rush**: unable to sleep, unable to stop building.
S2.quote: I'm afraid of becoming the reason my family's small savings disappear.
fieldNote: Adaptive: acts first and plans a company within days.
Aware the **window** for human help is short and says so honestly.
Fear is about his **parents' savings**, not about himself.

steps.text: Start a small company setting up AI for local shops
Automate the company's bookings and invoices with AI agents
Keep the option of his parents' spare room open
Post and sign petitions for a basic income trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something and short enough to be urgent. I'd tell my Discord that this is the time to make friends in the field and learn the things the machines can't handle yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's my best case. I'd have time to finish the master's, work two or three years in industry, and start putting money away. I might even be early enough to run something small before the big companies take it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job I can get and join an open source project on the side. I'd put away 300 a month and pay the debt down faster than the schedule. And I'd learn some hardware basics too, since robots come three years later and someone has to wire them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. A few knots, but they're the useful kind that make me move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why open source on the side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's visible proof of skill, and it's where the people with real jobs hang out. It cost me nothing but evenings. An open source project taught me more about working in a team than my entire degree did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the three years of robots after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd treat them as a gap year for hands-on work. The skills near machines are worth more during that gap. Beyond that, I honestly don't know, and I'd say that to anyone who claims they do.

say: Five years is long enough to **build** and short enough to be urgent.
This is the time to make **friends** in the field.
think: This is my **best case**: a master's, then two or three industry years.
I might run **something small** before the big firms take over.
do: **Take** the first job offered and join an open source project.
Save **300 a month** and pay the debt down faster.
Learn **hardware basics**, since robots arrive three years later.
feel: **Good** mostly, with useful knots that keep me moving.
S3.quote: An open source project taught me more about working in a team than my entire degree did.
fieldNote: Adaptive and optimistic, so a five-year window reads as an **opportunity**.
Honest about not knowing what comes **after** the robot gap.
Joins open source for visibility and **teamwork**.

steps.text: Take the first software job offer and start within the year
Put away 300 a month and overpay the loan
Do an evening course on embedded hardware and sensors
Contribute weekly to an open source project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the gift. I'd tell people to treat it like the decade before smartphones took over, when the ones who got ready did well. I'd also tell my Discord that learning how to learn is the main thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel confident. I'd be 34 with ten years of building behind me, probably a few contacts, maybe even my own small firm. I'd still be aware that none of it is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in industry for three years, then try my own product. I'd save in an index fund every month and keep my skills fresh with a new project each year. I'd keep helping students on Discord, because it keeps my network alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It feels like a long road with a good view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'none of it is guaranteed' mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd keep a cushion. If AGI arrives on time, even a strong decade of experience may not hold. I'd rather be someone with six months of savings and a spare plan than someone with a fancy title and no room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the Discord matter that much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, because my friends there are my safety net. Three of them have already offered to hire me if they start a firm, and I'd do the same for them. It's the kind of help no scheme gives you.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, like the decade before smartphones.
Learning **how to learn** is the main skill.
think: I'd feel **confident**, with ten years of building behind me.
None of it is **guaranteed**, so a cushion matters.
do: **Work** three years in industry, then try my own product.
Put money into an **index fund** every month.
Keep **helping students** on Discord to keep my network.
feel: **Calm** and curious, like a long road with a view.
S4.quote: I'd rather be someone with six months of savings and a spare plan than someone with a fancy title and no room to move.
fieldNote: Adaptive mindset plus a long window gives him real **confidence**.
Keeps a **cushion** anyway, which keeps him grounded.
His Discord friends are his **safety net**, a peer support idea.

steps.text: Work three years in industry before launching a product
Put 100 a month into an index fund
Keep six months of expenses as a cash cushion
Build one new project every year to stay current

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because even I would struggle to keep up. What would help is a basic income that starts before the job losses and public computing so more people can use the tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Perhaps that being excited isn't the same as being safe. I use AI every day and love it, but I know my own job could be one of the things it does well.

headlineQuote: I use AI every day and love it, but I know my own job could be one of the things it does well.
portrait: Bilal is 24, doing a master's in **artificial intelligence** after a pass in computer science.
He lives in a student block near **Redfield** University and tutors for pocket money.
Progressive and adaptive, he uses AI **every day** and runs a 200-member Discord for students.
He owes about 10,000 and has two months of savings, with his **parents** as backup.
He moves from uneasy to calm, and becomes anxious when the **entry-level rung** shrinks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because even fast adapters would struggle.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** before job losses and public computing access for all.
